summary: Describes the role of link indications, information from the link layer to higher layers about link state, in the Internet architecture. Used well, they can improve performance, but misuse can hurt robustness and performance. The memo summarizes proposals and architectural issues. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A link indication is a message from the wireless or wired link up to the layers above saying what the link is doing: up, down, fast, slow, lossy. The memo explains how the different layers should use such messages, and where using them wrongly makes the network slower or less reliable than ignoring them.

questions: how should higher layers use link layer information
what are the security risks of link indications
why is link up not the same as link down
subtitle: How the link layer can tell higher layers about the link, without making the Internet worse.

tldr.problem: The link layer knows things the Internet layer cannot see, such as the link's rate, its delay and its frame error rate, and using that knowledge can speed things up. But used carelessly it can also break robustness, congestion control and interoperability.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines link indications, describes a layered model in which the Internet layer filters them, the transport layer uses them for estimating path parameters and the application layer mostly ignores them, and then sets out eleven principles a proposal has to follow, with advice on models, definitions, robustness, races and transport.
tldr.outcome: This is guidance for document authors, not a specification. It is an IAB Informational memo from June 2007 that has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: Links with loss differing by direction

today: RFC 4907 is an Informational memo published by the Internet Architecture Board in June 2007, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is guidance for document authors rather than a specification, so it sets no protocol behaviour; its survey of the literature reflects the state of the work at that time.

sections.title: What Link Indications Are and Where They Came From
sections.content:
A link indication is information the link layer passes up to higher layers about the state of the link. The Internet architecture has used them for a long time. The ARPANET link layer protocol provided a "Destination Dead" indication when a send to an offline host failed, described in RFC 816. The ARPANET packet radio experiment folded frame loss into the calculation of routing metrics, a precursor to link-aware metrics such as the Expected Transmission Count. RIP and OSPF use the "Link Up" and "Link Down" indications that links provide, while also being able to detect link loss from the absence of routing packets. Later work went further: an experimental link control protocol defined states such as Down, Coming Up, Up, Going Down, Bring Down and Bring Up, a generalized model of link layer triggers defined Link Up, Link Down, Link Going Down, Link Going Up, Link Quality Crosses Threshold, Trigger Rollback and Better Signal Quality AP Available, and IEEE 802.21 defines a Media Independent Handover Event Service reporting on link characteristics, link status and link quality, with events including Link Down, Link Up, Link Going Down, Link Signal Strength and Link Signal/Noise Ratio.

Under ideal conditions a link that is up has low frame loss in both directions and can send and receive immediately, and a link that is down cannot do either. Real links are messier. Wired links can fail in half-duplex mode or show partial impairment with an intermediate loss rate. Wireless links can be asymmetric, can lose frames intermittently, and can change throughput quickly because of interference or signal fading. In both kinds of link the state can flap rapidly between up and down, and that behaviour is what makes integrating link indications into the Internet, transport and application layers difficult.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea is old: the ARPANET already told the layer above when a destination was dead. Today wireless links can also report their signal strength, their speed and how much they are losing packets. The memo says those reports are useful, but only if the layers above use them carefully.

sections.title: The Layered Indication Model
sections.content:
The RFC's model assumes the link layer hands up abstract indications that do not depend on the link technology. One of the Internet layer's jobs is to shield higher layers from the specifics of link behaviour, so it validates and filters link indications and chooses the outgoing and incoming interface from routing metrics. The routing table can be built from local interface information and from what routers tell it, with prefixes added or removed on the basis of DHCP, Router Advertisements, redirect messages or route updates. A "Link Up" indication makes the host validate its possible IP configurations, using a bidirectional reachability test in IPv4 and reachability detection with Router Solicitation and Advertisement in IPv6, but a Link Up need not change the Internet layer configuration at all.

The transport layer treats link indications differently for parameter estimation and for connection management. For parameter estimation it cares about path properties that affect performance, so rate, delay and frame loss can be used directly, and strict layering is deliberately relaxed here so the transport layer can use all available information. A "Link Down" followed later by a "Link Up" can suggest that packets were lost for reasons other than congestion, even when the IP configuration did not change and no Internet layer indication was sent. For connection management, though, layering is respected: the transport layer does not tear down a connection on a "Link Down" indication, because such an indication may be transient, or may be followed quickly by a "Link Up". Robustness comes from leaving connections up until an endpoint address changes or repeated retransmissions go unanswered. A change of Care-of Address under Mobile IP does not tear down the connection, because the mobility layer masks it.

Applications usually do not need link indications at all, because they can get what they need more reliably from the Internet and transport layers. A "Link Up" means the link can carry IP packets, not that the interface is configured, so applications should use an Internet layer "IP Address Configured" event instead. "Link Down" is rarely useful to applications because it is often followed quickly by "Link Up", so applications should react to transport layer teardown instead. That is why the model does not show link indications going directly to applications.
sections.plainLanguage: Each layer treats the same message differently. The Internet layer checks it and decides which interface to use. The transport layer uses it to estimate the path but never to close a connection. Applications are told to ignore it and watch for higher-layer events instead.

sections.title: Eleven Principles and the First Two Rules
sections.content:
Because real links behave badly, the RFC offers eleven principles for proposals that use link indications. In short: avoid simplified link models where they do not apply; define link indications clearly so it is understood when each one is generated; prove robustness against spurious indications and give upper layers a timely recovery step; prove that congestion control still works; prove that the optimization is actually worth it; never require link indications, so that link independence is kept; avoid race conditions from several layers using the same indication; avoid inconsistencies between link and routing metrics; do not let overhead reduction break interoperability or pull link dependencies up into the Internet and transport layers; and, for anything carried beyond the local host, think hard about layering, security and transport.

The first principle concerns models. Research on wireless networks warns that mistaken assumptions about link behaviour lead to protocols that do not work in practice, and the three-dimensional nature of wireless propagation can cause large signal strength changes over short distances, which shows up as rapid changes in rate, frame loss and signal strength. Two-state Markov models assume a link is either up with low loss or down with few frames delivered, and usually assume the two directions behave the same, which may be wrong when loss rates are intermediate. Signal strength data is also noisy and sometimes inconsistent, so it needs filtering, and the advice is to combine it with other signs of loss such as the absence of beacons. A document describing a capability that depends on link indications should say what its link model assumes and when it applies.

The second principle is clear definitions. Considerable work has gone into defining "Link Up" and "Link Down" and saying when each link layer sends them, and the advice is not to assume symmetric performance that is either low or high loss. A "Link Up" event should be sent because the link layer state changed, not because of transient conditions, and it may arrive late, since a large handoff latency delays it. Indications should be sensitive to transient conditions only where unavoidable, and should be built with damping where possible: the events are generated by the link layer state machine from real exchanges, such as completion of the IEEE 802.11i four-way handshake for Link Up or receipt of a PPP LCP-Terminate for Link Down, or by protracted frame loss that convinces the link layer the link is unusable. Finally, no assumption should be made that a "Link Down" event is sent at all, or sent in time. A good implementation detects connectivity failure quickly, for instance by tracking missing beacons, but only announces Link Down when it concludes the link is unusable.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo lists eleven rules for anyone who wants to build on link indications. The first two matter most: do not assume a simple picture of the link that is wrong outdoors or in a mesh network, and be precise about when a link is declared up or down, because everything above depends on that meaning.

sections.title: Robustness, Damping and Congestion Control
sections.content:
Robustness against misleading indications has three parts: variation between implementations, recovery from indications that turn out to be invalid, and damping and hysteresis. Implementation variation matters because radio propagation and implementation differences change how reliable indications are. Measurements from a 38-node urban multi-hop 802.11 ad-hoc network found that links which were very bad in one direction tended to be bad in both and links which were very good in one direction tended to be good in both, but 30 percent of links had loss rates differing substantially in each direction. Because wireless links often show loss rates between up and down and can be strongly asymmetric, a "Link Up" indication does not necessarily mean the link is reachable in both directions, since it may have been produced by exchanging small frames at low rates. The recommended answer is to treat an indication as a hint rather than a trigger, and to validate it. Detecting Network Attachment in IPv4 rate-limits Link Up indications and confirms bidirectional reachability before activating a configuration, while IPv4 Link-Local address configuration requires a claim-and-defend protocol, so a host returning from sleep must not reuse a formerly configured address without rerunning it.

Recovery from invalid indications matters too. Where the transport layer recovers from a bad indication, the recovered parameters, such as the Maximum Segment Size, the round-trip time, the retransmission timeout, the bandwidth and the congestion window, should be shown to remain valid. An example of what goes wrong comes from early IPv4 Link-Local implementations, which waited five minutes before trying to get a routable address; where mobile hosts changed their point of attachment more often than that, they never obtained one, because an invalid Link Up, signalling before link layer authentication had finished, caused the first attempt to fail. For the same reason RFC 3927 recommends against changing the 64-second maximum retransmission timeout given for DHCP.

Damping and hysteresis limit the damage from unstable indications, by damping them or by constraining how often indication-driven actions may occur within a period. The benefit has to be weighed against the added latency: a spurious "Link Down" may need to be held back until it is clear that no "Link Up" will follow, though where several beacons are missed there is no evidence of a suitable point of attachment nearby and no delay is needed. Sometimes indications should be ignored altogether, for example when a host moves from an ad-hoc network to one with centralised address management and cannot conclude from a Link Up that it should configure a link-local address.

Congestion control is the last piece. Proposals must show that effective congestion control is maintained, and several techniques are offered: rate limiting packets generated by an indication, for instance to one packet per path retransmission timeout; depending on upper-layer indications such as IP address configuration changes rather than on Link Up; using keepalives or connection teardown instead of consuming Link Down; and showing the proposal is not vulnerable to congestive collapse. The link layer also has to tell congestion loss apart from channel loss, because lowering the transmission rate in response to frame loss increases contention and can lead to collapse, so only loss from deteriorating channel conditions may be used to lower the rate. A host that retransmits its last packet on every Link Up could, on a rapidly moving node, produce a burst of retransmissions and break the principle of conservation of packets; the same applies to presence applications that register on Link Up and deregister on Link Down.
sections.plainLanguage: Real wireless links are messy, so the memo says treat what the link reports as a hint, not a command. Check it, have a way to undo a bad decision quickly, and do not let one report cause a burst of extra traffic.

sections.title: Effectiveness, Interoperability and Races
sections.content:
A proposal must show that its optimization works, because optimizations add complexity and need a substantial performance improvement to be worth it. With unreliable indications the result depends on the cost of false positives against false negatives. Detecting Network Attachment in IPv4 has modest benefits but a lengthy timeout as the penalty for failing to confirm a configuration, so the recommended strategy is to test several candidate configurations in parallel alongside DHCP, which makes the method always at least as good as DHCP alone. Link indications may be used where available but must never be required by upper layers, so that link independence is kept and hosts that do not understand a hint can still obtain an address. Where indications are proposed to optimise IP configuration they must not compromise robustness by interfering with address assignment or routing behaviour or with Duplicate Address Detection, and interoperability has to remain possible, even with degraded performance, if some participants do not implement the proposal.

Race conditions appear when several layers of the stack use the same indication directly. In a Weak End System host, where addresses refer to hosts rather than interfaces, a change of outgoing interface can happen at the same moment as the transport layer is adjusting its parameters, so behaviour can depend on the order in which the indications are processed. A multi-homed host that sees rising frame loss on one interface raises the routing metric for that interface, which may change the outgoing interface and trigger Mobile IP signalling to change the incoming path as well, leaving the parameters estimated for the old path, such as the congestion state or the Maximum Segment Size, invalid for the new one. Three remedies are given. Reset the transport parameters when the Internet layer detects a path change, so that estimates from the old path do not persist. Rely on layering, so that the Internet layer dampens transient indications and applications use Internet or transport layer indications instead. And keep the link and routing metrics consistent, because differences between the indications used for routing and those used for roaming can cause instability, especially in multi-homed hosts.

The metrics themselves have limits. The Expected Transmission Count metric, based on frame loss before retransmission, selects routes that maximise throughput where the transmission rate is constant, but where the rate varies the Expected Transmission Time metric is better, being a bandwidth-adjusted ETX, and it in turn underestimates the cost at higher rates because it assumes the loss fraction of small probe frames sent at 1 Mbps predicts the loss fraction of larger frames. Signal strength and access point load can help decide where to attach, but signal strength is a poor predictor of loss or throughput because of multi-path interference, and an access point with low utilisation may simply be broken. Reducing overhead by combining exchanges from several layers is also risky: advertising prefixes in the 802.11 Beacon and Probe Response frames can hand the host the wrong address, because the VLAN identifier may be assigned dynamically after the advertisement was made. And proposals to carry link indications beyond the local host must show they are better than implicit signals, which need no new packets, work better with middleboxes, and are less likely to create security holes.
sections.plainLanguage: An optimization has to earn its keep, and it must not become something the network depends on, or a set of instructions that two layers follow at once and disagree about. The memo also warns that the usual wireless measures, signal strength and access point load, are poor guides to how well a link will actually carry data.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Proposals that use link indications can create new holes, and the RFC groups them as spoofing, indication validation and denial of service. Where link layer control frames are unprotected they can be spoofed: PPP does not protect LCP frames such as LCP-Terminate, and IEEE 802.11 does not protect management frames such as Associate, Reassociate, Disassociate or Deauthenticate. Spoofing these can exploit weaknesses in a proposal, and a proposal without congestion avoidance can let an attacker mount a denial-of-service attack. Even where the link layer has security, an inconsistent model leaves gaps: 802.11i stations cannot send or receive IP packets until the four-way handshake completes, so a link implementing it cannot count as usable at the Internet layer until then, but 802.11i does not authenticate management frames. That weakness lets an attacker disassociate a station anywhere in the network by sending an unauthenticated Reassociation Request.

On validation, the RFC quotes the old advice that a host should ask the gateway for advice and believe it, while noting that in today's security environment it is inadvisable to act on indications from routers without careful consideration, because ICMP error messages can be forged to abort connections, block new ones or slow existing ones. Transported link indications are typically unauthenticated, so a receiving host may not be able to tell whether they are authentic or even plausible. Where a proposal reacts to unauthenticated link layer frames it should use upper-layer security where possible: a host that used an unauthenticated control frame to conclude that a link is operational can still use SEND or authenticated DHCP to obtain secure Internet layer configuration.

Denial of service is the third area. Wireless links are naturally vulnerable to interference, but such an attack needs radio contact with the target network, while attacks mounted from a distance, by another host on the same network or by an off-link attacker, widen the exposure. Transporting link indications can make a local weakness usable across the Internet. Because upper layers now validate indications, they should not spend excessive resources doing it. Congestion control is a security matter as well as a transport matter: a single forged link layer frame should not produce a magnified response, whether that is several responses or one larger one, and proposals should not let several hosts answer a frame sent to a multicast address.
sections.plainLanguage: Because link control frames are often unprotected, somebody can fake them. The memo's warnings are that a faked report should not make a host send a storm of packets, that a link which claims to be up should still be configured securely at the IP layer, and that carrying link reports across the Internet would turn a local weakness into a remote one.

viz.caption: THE LAYERS AND WHAT EACH ONE DOES WITH LINK INDICATIONS

layers.label: Application
layers.detail: Uses IP address configured and connection teardown events, not raw link indications

layers.label: Transport
layers.detail: Uses indications to estimate path parameters, never to tear down a connection

layers.label: Internet
layers.detail: Validates and filters indications, picks interfaces from routing metrics

layers.label: Link
layers.detail: Produces link state, rate, delay and frame error rate

viz.caption: THE KINDS OF LINK INDICATION THE RFC NAMES

items.title: Link Up
items.text: The interface has become able to communicate data frames.

items.title: Link Down
items.text: The interface is no longer able to communicate data frames.

items.title: Link Going Down
items.text: A warning that the link is about to fail.

items.title: Link Going Up
items.text: A warning that the link is about to come back.

items.title: Link Signal Strength
items.text: How strong the received signal is.

items.title: Link Signal/Noise Ratio
items.text: Signal strength compared with background noise.

items.title: Link Quality Crosses Threshold
items.text: Quality has passed a chosen limit.

items.title: Better Signal Quality AP Available
items.text: A nearby access point offers a better link.
